intro: Hindu families keep many festivals. Two big ones are Diwali and Holi. Diwali is the festival of lights. Holi is the festival of colors.
Festivals come with stories. The stories often teach values. You will learn namaste, ahimsa and seva. All children can talk about these ideas.
By the end, you can say how families get ready for Diwali. You can tell about Holi and Prahlada. You can name ways to be kind.
bigQuestion: How do festivals and stories help people be kind?

timeline.t: In autumn, a family cleans the house for Diwali
Children make a rangoli pattern by the door
The family lights little clay diyas
Many families do a Lakshmi puja and share sweets
In spring, people light a bonfire the night before Holi
Friends throw colored powder and make up
People greet each other with namaste
Neighbors do seva and help each other

words.d: the festival of lights in the autumn
a small clay lamp with oil and a wick
a colorful pattern made on the floor with powder, rice or petals
a time of worship, with offerings like flowers and lamps
the spring festival of colors
a greeting with hands pressed together and a small bow
not hurting any living thing
helping others without asking for anything back

write.prompt: Draw and tell. Pick Diwali or Holi. Draw one thing families do. Tell a grown-up what they do and what many families say it means.
tips: Say "Many families say..." when you tell what it means.
Use a word from this unit, like diya, rangoli or seva.

title: Lights, Colors and Kindness

chapters.title: Diwali: The Festival of Lights
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do so many families light lamps at Diwali?

story.title: A Flower by the Door
story.kicker: A girl draws a rangoli flower by the front door and sets a tiny lamp in the middle.
paragraphs: It is a cool autumn evening. Priya kneels by her front door. She has little bowls of colored powder. Red, yellow, green and blue.
She pinches some red powder. She lets it fall in a curvy line. Line by line, a big flower grows. Her grandma helps with the petals.
Then Priya holds a tiny clay lamp. Her dad lights it for her. She sets it in the middle of the flower. The little flame dances.
"Now the house is ready," says Grandma. "Happy Diwali!" Inside, the whole family is getting ready for the festival of lights.
story.think: Priya made something beautiful to welcome people. How does your family get ready for a special day?

lessons.title: What Is Diwali?
lessons.mainIdea: Diwali is a festival of lights in the autumn.
reading: *Diwali* is a festival of lights. It comes in the autumn, in October or November. In many places it lasts five days.
Families clean their homes. They light lamps. They wear new clothes. They visit family and share sweets. It is a very happy time.

words.d: the festival of lights in the autumn
the season when leaves fall; also called fall

look.title: Five Happy Days
look.text: Look at the calendar on the fridge. Five days in a row have little stars. A boy points to the middle day. "That is the big night of lights," his mom says.
look.prompt: Why might a festival last more than one day?

check.q: What is Diwali?
check.why: Diwali is the festival of lights.

check.q: When is Diwali?
check.why: Diwali comes in the autumn, in October or November.

check.q: What do families share at Diwali?
check.why: Families share sweets at Diwali.

lessons.title: Little Clay Lamps
lessons.mainIdea: Families light little clay lamps called diyas.
reading: A *diya* is a small clay lamp. It holds oil and a cotton wick. Families light many diyas at Diwali.
They set diyas by doors and windows. They set them on steps. The whole house glows in the dark night.

words.d: a small clay lamp with oil and a wick

look.title: Rows of Lights
look.text: Look at the steps of the house. A diya sits on each step. Tiny flames flicker in a row. The windows glow gold. The night is dark, but the house is bright.
look.prompt: How does the house look different with all the lamps?

check.q: What is a diya?
check.why: A diya is a small clay lamp.

check.q: What does a diya hold?
check.why: A diya holds oil and a cotton wick.

check.q: Where do families set diyas?
check.why: Families set diyas by doors, windows and steps.

lessons.title: Different Stories, One Festival
lessons.mainIdea: Hindu families remember different stories at Diwali.
reading: Many Hindus remember Rama and Sita coming home. People lit lamps to welcome them. Other Hindus honor Lakshmi. She is the goddess of good fortune.
In South India, many remember a story of Krishna. The stories are different. The lights are the same.

words.d: the goddess of good fortune, honored by many Hindus at Diwali

look.title: Two Friends, Two Stories
look.text: Look at two friends at school. Asha says, "At Diwali, we remember Rama coming home." Dev says, "At Diwali, my family honors Lakshmi." They both smile. They both light lamps.
look.prompt: Can two families keep the same festival with different stories? How?

check.q: Whose homecoming do many Hindus remember at Diwali?
check.why: Many Hindus remember Rama and Sita coming home.

check.q: Who is Lakshmi?
check.why: Many Hindus honor Lakshmi as the goddess of good fortune.

check.q: Do all Hindu families tell the same Diwali story?
check.why: Hindu families remember different stories at Diwali.

lessons.title: Lakshmi Puja
lessons.mainIdea: Many families honor Lakshmi with a puja on Diwali night.
reading: A *puja* is a time of worship. On Diwali night, many families do a Lakshmi puja. They gather at the home shrine.
They offer flowers, lamps and sweets. They sing. Many say Lakshmi is welcome in a clean, bright home.

words.d: a time of worship, with offerings like flowers and lamps

look.title: Lakshmi on the Lotus
look.text: The old texts describe Lakshmi rising from the ocean, seated on a lotus flower and holding lotus flowers.
look.cite: Retold from the Vishnu Purana, Book 1, chapter 9

check.q: What is a puja?
check.why: A puja is a time of worship with offerings.

check.q: Who do many families honor on Diwali night?
check.why: Many families do a Lakshmi puja on Diwali night.

check.q: What flower goes with Lakshmi?
check.why: The Vishnu Purana describes Lakshmi seated on a lotus.

lessons.title: Diwali for Sikhs and Jains
lessons.mainIdea: Sikhs and Jains keep Diwali too, for their own reasons.
reading: Hindus are not the only people who keep Diwali. Sikhs light lamps too. They remember Guru Hargobind being set free.
Jains keep Diwali too. They remember their great teacher Mahavira. Each faith has its own reason. Each lights lamps.

words.d: a person who follows the Sikh faith
a person who follows the Jain faith

look.title: Who Keeps Diwali?
look.cite: Common reference works on Indian religions
look.prompt: How many faiths on this list light lamps at Diwali?

check.q: Which faiths keep Diwali besides Hindus?
check.why: Sikhs and Jains keep Diwali too.

check.q: Who do Sikhs remember at Diwali time?
check.why: Sikhs remember Guru Hargobind being set free.

check.q: Who do Jains remember at Diwali?
check.why: Jains remember their teacher Mahavira.

lessons.title: Rangoli Patterns
lessons.mainIdea: Families make rangoli patterns to welcome guests.
reading: *Rangoli* is a pattern made on the floor. People use colored powder, rice or flower petals.
Families make rangoli by the door. It says, "Welcome!" Many rangoli have flowers, dots, lines and circles.

words.d: a colorful pattern made on the floor with powder, rice or petals

look.title: A Pattern Grows
look.text: Look at the rangoli. It starts with dots in rows. Next come lines that join the dots. Then petals fill the spaces. Last, a diya goes in the middle.
look.prompt: What shapes can you see in a rangoli? Name two.

check.q: What is rangoli?
check.why: Rangoli is a colorful pattern on the floor.

check.q: What can rangoli be made of?
check.why: People use colored powder, rice or flower petals.

check.q: What does rangoli by the door say?
check.why: Rangoli by the door welcomes guests.

lessons.title: Diwali in Illinois
lessons.mainIdea: Hindu families in Illinois celebrate Diwali too.
reading: Many Hindu families live in Illinois. They celebrate Diwali at home. Many go to a temple too.
The Hindu Temple of Greater Chicago is in Lemont. Families visit temples like it at Diwali. Some schools share Diwali with their classes.

words.d: a building where people gather to worship

look.title: A Family Gets Ready
look.text: Step 1: Clean the house. Step 2: Put on new clothes. Step 3: Make rangoli by the door. Step 4: Light the diyas. Step 5: Share sweets with family and friends.
look.prompt: Which step would you like to help with? Why?

check.q: Do Hindu families in Illinois celebrate Diwali?
check.why: Many Hindu families in Illinois celebrate Diwali.

check.q: Where is the Hindu Temple of Greater Chicago?
check.why: The Hindu Temple of Greater Chicago is in Lemont, Illinois.

check.q: What is one way to get ready for Diwali?
check.why: Many families clean the house before Diwali.

lessons.title: Light Over Dark
lessons.mainIdea: Many families say Diwali's lights stand for good winning over bad.
reading: At Diwali, lamps shine in the dark. Many families say this is a sign. Light wins over darkness.
Many say it also means good wins over bad. Kindness wins over meanness. The lights help people remember.

words.d: something that stands for an idea

look.title: One Small Flame
look.text: Look at the dark room. It is very dark. Then someone lights one small diya. Now you can see faces. You can see smiles.
look.prompt: What can one small light do in a dark room?

check.q: What do many say Diwali's lights stand for?
check.why: Many families say the lights stand for good winning over bad.

check.q: What is a sign?
choices: Something that stands for an idea
check.why: A sign stands for an idea.

check.q: What wins over darkness at Diwali?
check.why: Families say light wins over darkness.

review.why: Diwali is the festival of lights.
A diya is a small clay lamp.
Rangoli is a colorful pattern made on the floor.

review.q: Who is honored in a Lakshmi puja?
review.why: Many families honor Lakshmi on Diwali night.
Sikhs and Jains keep Diwali for their own reasons.

review.q: What do many say the lights stand for?
review.why: Many say Diwali's lights stand for good winning over bad.

chapters.title: Holi, Namaste and Helping Others
chapters.bigQuestion: How can we be kind to people and to every living thing?

story.title: Colors in the Air
story.kicker: Pink and green powder fills the air, and two old friends laugh and hug.
paragraphs: It is spring. The sun is warm again. Children run into the park with bags of colored powder. Pink, green, yellow and blue.
Arjun sees his friend Meera across the grass. Last week they had a fight. They did not talk for days. Arjun feels a little shy.
Meera smiles. She tosses a puff of pink powder at him. Arjun laughs. He tosses green powder back. Soon they are both covered in color.
"Happy Holi!" they shout. They hug. Many families say Holi is a day to make up with friends. Arjun and Meera are friends again.
story.think: Arjun and Meera made up. What helps you make up with a friend?

lessons.title: A Spring Festival
lessons.mainIdea: Holi is a happy spring festival of colors.
reading: *Holi* is a festival of colors. It comes in the spring, in March in many years. It welcomes the warm days.
People throw colored powder. They spray colored water. They sing and dance. They share sweets and food.

words.d: the spring festival of colors

look.title: A Rainbow Crowd
look.text: Look at the people in the street. Their white shirts are now pink, green and blue. Their faces are yellow and purple. Everyone is laughing.
look.prompt: Name three colors you see in this picture.

check.q: What is Holi?
check.why: Holi is the spring festival of colors.

check.q: When is Holi?
check.why: Holi comes in the spring.

check.q: What do people throw at Holi?
check.why: People throw colored powder at Holi.

lessons.title: Making Up With Friends
lessons.mainIdea: Many families say Holi is a time to make up and start fresh.
reading: At Holi, everyone is covered in color. You cannot tell who is who! Many families say this helps people feel equal.
Many say Holi is a time to forgive. Friends make up after fights. Neighbors share food. It is a fresh start.

words.d: to stop being angry with someone

look.title: A Fresh Start
look.text: Look at two neighbors. Last year they argued about a fence. Today one brings the other a plate of sweets. "Happy Holi," she says. The other one smiles.
look.prompt: Why is a festival a good time to make up?

check.q: What do many say Holi is a time to do?
check.why: Many families say Holi is a time to forgive.

check.q: What does forgive mean?
choices: To stop being angry with someone
check.why: To forgive is to stop being angry.

check.q: Why can't you tell who is who at Holi?
check.why: At Holi, color covers everyone.

lessons.title: The Boy Who Stayed Brave
lessons.mainIdea: Prahlada stayed brave and kind, even when it was hard.
reading: Prahlada was a prince. He loved Vishnu with all his heart. Many Hindus honor Vishnu as God.
His father was a proud king. He wanted everyone to honor only him. Prahlada said no, kindly. He kept loving Vishnu. He stayed brave.

words.d: a boy in the stories who stays brave and loyal to Vishnu
honored by many Hindus as God who protects the world

look.title: Prahlada Stays True
look.text: Prahlada's father tries many times to make him stop honoring Vishnu. Each time Prahlada stays calm and true, and each time he is kept safe.
look.cite: Retold from the Bhagavata Purana, Book 7, chapters 5 to 8
look.prompt: How does Prahlada act when his father is angry?

check.q: Who did Prahlada love with all his heart?
check.why: The Bhagavata Purana says Prahlada loved Vishnu.

check.q: What did Prahlada's father want?
check.why: His proud father wanted to be honored above all.

check.q: How did Prahlada act?
check.why: Prahlada stayed brave and kind.

lessons.title: The Bonfire
lessons.mainIdea: Many people light a bonfire the night before Holi to remember Prahlada.
reading: In a well-known Holi story, Prahlada is kept safe from a great fire. His cruel aunt Holika is not.
So the night before Holi, many people light a big bonfire. They remember that Prahlada was kept safe. They say good wins over bad.

words.d: a big outdoor fire

look.title: Around the Fire
look.text: Look at the families around the bonfire. It is night. The fire crackles. The grown-ups keep the children at a safe distance. They tell the story of Prahlada.
look.prompt: Why do families tell a story around the fire?

check.q: When do many people light the Holi bonfire?
check.why: Many light a bonfire the night before Holi.

check.q: Who is kept safe in the story?
check.why: In the Holi story, Prahlada is kept safe.

check.q: What do people say the bonfire shows?
choices: Fire is fun to play with
check.why: Many say the bonfire shows good winning over bad.

lessons.title: Namaste
lessons.mainIdea: Namaste is a greeting with hands pressed together.
reading: *Namaste* is a greeting. You press your hands together. You bow your head a little. Many Hindus greet people this way.
Many explain namaste as honoring the good in the other person. It is a kind, gentle way to say hello.

words.d: a greeting with hands pressed together and a small bow

look.title: Saying Hello
look.text: Look at the grandpa at the door. A guest arrives. The grandpa presses his hands together. He bows a little. "Namaste," he says. The guest does the same.
look.prompt: What are different ways people say hello? Name two.

check.q: What is namaste?
check.why: Namaste is a greeting with hands together.

check.q: How do people hold their hands for namaste?
check.why: For namaste, people press their hands together.

check.q: How do many explain namaste?
choices: Honoring the good in the other person
check.why: Many explain namaste as honoring the good in others.

lessons.title: Ahimsa: Not Hurting
lessons.mainIdea: Ahimsa means not hurting any living thing.
reading: *Ahimsa* is an old word. It means not hurting. Not hurting people. Not hurting animals. Not hurting any living thing.
Many Hindus, Jains and Buddhists teach ahimsa. Some families eat no meat because of it. Mahatma Gandhi made ahimsa famous.

words.d: not hurting any living thing

look.title: A Great Duty
look.text: The Mahabharata calls not hurting others the highest duty.
look.cite: Retold from the Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva (Book 13)
look.prompt: What does this old book say is the highest duty?

check.q: What does ahimsa mean?
check.why: Ahimsa means not hurting any living thing.

check.q: Who made ahimsa famous?
check.why: Mahatma Gandhi made ahimsa famous around the world.

check.q: Why do some families eat no meat?
check.why: Some families eat no meat to follow ahimsa.

lessons.title: Seva: Helping Others
lessons.mainIdea: Seva means helping others without asking for anything back.
reading: *Seva* means helping others. You help without asking for a reward. Many Hindus and Sikhs do seva.
Some cook and serve free meals at a temple. Some clean a park. Some help a neighbor. Every helper counts, like the little squirrel.

words.d: helping others without asking for anything back

look.title: Ways to Help
look.cite: Common forms of seva described by Hindu and Sikh communities
look.prompt: Which way to help could you do this week?

check.q: What is seva?
choices: Helping others without asking for a reward
check.why: Seva means helping others freely.

check.q: Where do some people serve free meals?
check.why: Some people serve free meals at a temple as seva.

check.q: Which story also shows that every helper counts?
check.why: The squirrel story shows every helper counts.

review.why: Holi is the spring festival of colors.

review.q: Who stayed brave and loved Vishnu?
review.why: Prahlada stayed brave and loved Vishnu.
Namaste is a greeting with hands pressed together.
Seva means helping others without asking for anything back.

review.q: What do many say Holi is a time to do?
review.why: Many say Holi is a time to forgive and make up.
